title: Weekly Recap: Critical CVEs, Linux DDoS Botnet, Device-Code Phishing, Android Spyware and More
summary: Some attacks this week didn't need much of a trick. A fake support call, a trusted extension, a shared link, or a device with no password. Small things that people barely think about. Yet each was enough to cause serious trouble.

title: Google Disrupts 1.3 Million-Device Android Botnet, Says TV Box Maker Sold Criminal Access
summary: A botnet of more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV set-top boxes, lost control of its servers in late October in a takedown led by Google.
card_summary: A botnet of more than 1.3 million Android devices, mostly TV set-top boxes, lost control of its servers in late October in a takedown led by Google.

sections.technical: Google says it is highly confident that device maker Videostrong intentionally put a backdoor in the boxes and sold access to criminals.

title: Critical Langflow Flaws Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Run Code on Servers
summary: Two critical flaws in Langflow could let a remote attacker with no account bypass authentication or run arbitrary code, IBM said last week.
card_summary: Two critical flaws in Langflow could let a remote attacker with no account bypass authentication or run arbitrary code, IBM said last week.

sections.mitigation: Every release from 1.0.0 through 1.12.8 has the flaws, and the only fix is version 1.13.0.

email_summary: Two critical flaws in Langflow could let a remote attacker with no account bypass authentication or run arbitrary code, IBM said last week. Severity is rated high.

title: Is Your SOC Ready for AI Agents? A Maturity Check Before You Deploy
summary: Forty percent of security teams now use AI every day, and another 56% are testing it. Only 4% have no plans to adopt it, according to Prophet Security's State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey of more than 250 CISOs, SOC leaders and practitioners. For the teams still testing, the next decision is whether their own SOC is ready.

title: Attackers Pose as IT Support on Microsoft Teams, Abuse AD CS to Steal Company Data
summary: Attackers posing as IT support on Microsoft Teams talked employees into giving them remote control of their PCs. They then used insecure Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) settings to obtain login certificates for privileged accounts, including one for a domain controller.

title: New VOLTA Infostealer Uses Claude, Gemini, and Kimi AI to Rank Victims by Financial Value
summary: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a new Windows infostealer malware called VOLTA-AUTODOXER (aka VOLTA) that makes use of a large language model (LLM) to rank a victim's stolen data by their monetization value.
card_summary: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a new Windows infostealer malware called VOLTA-AUTODOXER (aka VOLTA) that makes use of a large language model (LLM) to rank a victim's stolen data by their monetization value.

sections.context: This fits the broader data-exposure trend where follow-on abuse of leaked information is common.

email_summary: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a new Windows infostealer malware called VOLTA-AUTODOXER (aka VOLTA) that makes use of a large language model (LLM) to rank a victim's stolen data by their monetization value. Like other typical stealer families, VOLTA is equipped to harvest passwords and cookies from Chromium-based web browsers; data from Outlook profiles and Slack workspaces;.
